title: Sixteen Nights: KL to Angkor
summary: New Year's Eve under the Kuala Lumpur skyline, five days of temples and canals in Bangkok, the mountain temples of Chiang Mai, and four days among the ruins of Angkor.
principles: Your own day-by-day plan is the backbone; every stop you planned is kept unless it is closed on the day it falls on.
Ideas you scored 7–9 were slotted in where they sit next to something you had already planned, so they add little travel time.
Ideas you scored 4 or lower were dropped. Ideas you scored 5–6 appear as optional stops or in the backup list.
Days are deliberately overbooked. Optional stops (dashed numbers) are the first things to cut.
Days were checked against weekday opening rules — for example Chatuchak and Chiang Mai's Coconut Market are weekend-only, and Bangkok's National Museum is closed Monday and Tuesday.

cities.name: Siem Reap
cities.tagline: Angkor at sunrise on foot, the grand circuit by bike, and life on the Tonle Sap.

days.title: Arrival, Angkor pass and a balloon at sunset
days.summary: Fly in from Chiang Mai (via Bangkok; there is no direct flight), ride 50 minutes into town and settle in. In the late afternoon buy the 3-day Angkor pass dated for Monday: after 16:45 it also lets you into the park this evening for free. Watch sunset from the Angkor Balloon above Angkor Wat's moat, then wander the Old Market and eat on the riverside.
notes: Angkor pass plan: buy a 3-day pass with Mon 11 Jan as the start date. Holding a ticket dated for tomorrow lets you enter from 16:45 today for sunset, and this evening does not count as a pass day.

Use the 3 pass days on Mon 11 (SR2), Wed 13 (SR4) and either Thu 14 (sunrise before the airport, if your flight leaves after about 12:00) or Tue 12 (only if you swap Kompong Khleang for Phnom Krom sunset, which needs the pass). Kompong Khleang, the museum and the balloon do not need the pass.

The ticket counters on Road 60 close at 17:30. If your flight lands after about 15:00, buy the pass online beforehand (angkorenterprise.gov.kh, photo upload needed for multi-day passes) and skip the counter.
If you are tired or the balloon is not flying: skip it and go straight to the Old Market. Sunset can be seen from Srah Srang or Pre Rup (open to 19:00) using the free evening entry instead.

stops.name: Arrive at Siem Reap Angkor International Airport (SAI)
stops.description: Siem Reap's new airport (SAI) opened in October 2023, about 47 km east of town, replacing the old airport next to the temples. It is a large, quiet terminal with ATMs (USD), SIM card counters and a fixed-price taxi desk in arrivals. Cambodia issues visas on arrival (US$30, cash, passport photo) or you can get an e-Visa in advance. The road into town runs through flat rice country and takes 50–60 minutes.
tips: Get an e-Visa (evisa.gov.kh) before you fly to skip the visa-on-arrival queue.
Buy a local SIM (Smart, Cellcard or Metfone, about US$5–10 for plenty of data) in arrivals: Grab and PassApp need data.
The cheapest way in is the airport shuttle bus (about US$8, 60–70 min, ends at the CDF Duty Free shop near Wat Bo); the official taxi desk charges about US$25–35 per car; a hotel pickup is US$25–35.
Bring small, clean US dollar notes: torn or old notes are refused, and change under $1 comes back in riel.
stops.hours: Airport open for all flights; shuttle bus timetable from the airport (early 2025): 09:30, 11:00, 12:30, 15:00, 16:00, 17:00, 17:30, 20:00, 21:00, 22:00 — check on arrival
stops.cost: Shuttle US$8 (≈ 32,000 riel); taxi US$25–35; hotel pickup US$25–35
stops.from_previous: Flight from Chiang Mai via Bangkok (BKK with Bangkok Airways/Thai, or DMK with Thai AirAsia); about 4–7 h door to door including the connection

video.title: All You Need To Know To Arrive In Siem Reap Angkor Airport and Get To Town

stops.warning: No direct Chiang Mai–Siem Reap flight; you connect in Bangkok. The Thailand–Cambodia land border is closed.

stops.name: Buy the 3-day Angkor pass (Angkor Ticket Centre, Road 60)
stops.description: All of the Angkor Archaeological Park, plus Roluos, Banteay Srei, Beng Mealea and Phnom Krom, is covered by one pass sold by Angkor Enterprise. The 3-day pass (US$62) covers any 3 days within its validity window (7 days according to the 2026 ticket card; older guides say 10), so the days do not need to be consecutive. Multi-day passes carry your photo, taken by webcam at the counter or uploaded when you buy online. The counters are a large hall on Road 60, about 4 km north-east of the Old Market, on the way to the temples.
tips: After 16:45 you can buy a pass dated for tomorrow and enter the park this evening for sunset for free; the evening does not use a pass day.

Buying online (angkorenterprise.gov.kh or the Angkor Pass app) is the official alternative: pick Mon 11 Jan as the start date, upload a plain-background photo without glasses, and the QR code arrives by email.
Only angkorenterprise.gov.kh, the app, the kiosks and the Road 60 office sell valid tickets. Do not buy from resellers.
Keep the pass on you all day: it is scanned at the road checkpoints and at most temples.
stops.cost: 1-day US$37 · 3-day US$62 · 7-day US$72 (card or cash; ATM on site)
stops.from_previous: From the Old Market: tuk-tuk 10–15 min (about US$2–3 by Grab/PassApp), or walk 4.8 km (65 min)
stops.warning: Ticket counters close at 17:30; if you land late, buy online in advance.

stops.name: Angkor Balloon at sunset
stops.description: A tethered helium balloon that rises about 120–200 m on a cable from a field just west of Angkor Wat's moat and hangs there for 10–15 minutes. From the basket you see the five towers of Angkor Wat rising out of the forest inside their square moat, Phnom Bakheng on its hill, the West Baray reservoir and, on clear evenings, the Tonle Sap lake. It is a short, simple ride, not a hot-air balloon flight, but it is the only easy bird's-eye view of Angkor Wat. The launch site is outside the temple checkpoints, so no pass is needed.
tips: Look for the yellow balloon in the sky as you ride up: if it is not up, it is probably not flying (wind).
Aim for the last ride before sunset (~17:15–17:30): the light falls on Angkor Wat's west face, which is the side you look at.
Do not confuse it with the 'Angkor hot-air balloon' tours sold online, which are a different company and fly from the countryside at sunrise.
stops.hours: Sundays 05:15–18:15 (weekday hours are shorter); flights only in calm weather
stops.from_previous: From the ticket centre: tuk-tuk 15 min (7.5 km), about US$4–5

video.title: Riding a Hot Air Balloon Over Angkor Wat

stops.warning: The most recent reviews found are from late 2024; confirm it is operating (ask your hotel or tuk-tuk driver) before planning around it.

stops.name: Old Market (Psar Chas), riverside and dinner
stops.description: Psar Chas is the town's original covered market, built in the French colonial period near the Siem Reap river. By day it sells everything from dried fish and spices to silk scarves, silver and carvings; in the evening the food stalls and the streets around it fill up. Pub Street, The Lane and Alley West are a block away, with restaurants and bars, and the river path with its lit footbridges is a calm place to walk after dinner. It is a good first-night introduction to Siem Reap's easy-going pace.
tips: The inner market winds down around 18:00–19:00; come back by day (e.g. SR3) if you want to shop properly.
For Khmer food try fish amok, lok lak and num banh chok (rice noodles with green fish curry); Malis, Mahob and Chanrey Tree are well-known Khmer restaurants a short walk away.
Bargain at stalls (start around half the asking price, and smile).
Pub Street gets loud after 21:00; the riverside and Kandal Village (one block east) are quieter.
stops.hours: Market stalls ~07:00–19:00; restaurants and bars until late
stops.from_previous: From the balloon: tuk-tuk 15–20 min (7 km), about US$4–5

video.title: Siem Reap - Peaceful Morning Walk [4K, No Commentary]

days.title: Angkor Wat sunrise on foot, then east through the forest temples
days.summary: An early, long and memorable day. Walk out of town in the dark to Angkor Wat (about 7.5 km), watch the towers appear against the dawn sky, then explore the temple while most sunrise visitors leave for breakfast. Leave by the quiet east gate and walk through the forest to Ta Keo, Ta Prohm and Banteay Kdei, then lunch at Srah Srang. In the afternoon take a tuk-tuk for East Mebon and Pre Rup, and finish with sunset from Pre Rup.
notes: Changed: reordered to Angkor Wat → Ta Keo → Ta Prohm → Banteay Kdei/Srah Srang, because on foot this is a continuous line (Ta Keo is next to Ta Prohm's north gate, and Banteay Kdei is 600 m from Ta Prohm's east gate). The draft order would add about 3 km of backtracking.

Walking total to Srah Srang is about 20 km including walking inside the temples. Pre Rup, East Mebon and Banteay Samre are best by tuk-tuk (Pre Rup is 14 km from town). Arrange a pickup at Srah Srang the evening before, or use Grab/PassApp, which work on the main park roads.
Pass day 1 of 3. Sunrise 06:31, first colour from about 05:50; sunset 17:55.

Bakan (Angkor Wat's top level) is open today: it closes only on Buddhist holy days and on the afternoons of the 14th and 28th of each month. 11 Jan is not a holy day (new moon ~8 Jan, first-quarter holy day ~15 Jan).
If tired, cut in this order: Banteay Samre, East Mebon, then go back to town after Srah Srang lunch and skip the Pre Rup sunset.

stops.name: Angkor Wat at sunrise, then the temple itself
stops.description: Angkor Wat was built in the early 12th century by King Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu and probably his own tomb, and it is still the largest religious monument in the world. It faces west across a 190 m-wide moat; the classic sunrise view is from the two reflection pools inside the outer wall, with the five lotus-bud towers outlined against the sky. After sunrise, walk the first-floor galleries, which hold about 800 m of bas-reliefs (the Churning of the Ocean of Milk on the east side of the south gallery is the most famous), then climb to Bakan, the steep top level, for views over the forest. It is still an active Buddhist site, with monks and offerings in the cross-shaped Preah Poan galleries.
tips: Walking out: from the Old Market follow Charles de Gaulle Blvd north past the Angkor National Museum to the checkpoint at the moat's south-west corner, then along the moat to the west causeway: 7.5 km, about 1 h 35. Leave by 04:10. Wear a headlamp or reflective layer; the road has a wide shoulder but tuk-tuks speed past in the dark. If you stay north of town (near Raffles/Charles de Gaulle) it is 5–6 km.

In mid-January the sun rises well to the right (south) of the towers. Stand at the western edge of the left (north) pool for the classic towers-and-reflection shot; the right (south) pool has a similar view with fewer people.
Do not leave at 06:40 with the crowds: the galleries are almost empty from 07:00 to 08:30. Bakan opens around 07:40; shoulders and knees must be covered.
Breakfast: stalls opposite the west entrance and on the north side of the temple serve noodles, coffee and fruit (US$3–5).
stops.hours: Angkor Wat 05:00–18:00; Bakan (top level) ~07:40–17:00, open on Mon 11 Jan
stops.from_previous: On foot from the Old Market, 7.5 km, about 1 h 35 (or tuk-tuk 20 min, about US$5–8 one way before dawn)

video.title: ANGKOR WAT (Cambodia) | Largest Temple in the World | Full Tour & Documentary in 4K

stops.name: Ta Keo
stops.description: Ta Keo is a five-tower temple-mountain started around 1000 AD by King Jayavarman V and never finished: according to inscriptions it was struck by lightning, which was taken as a bad omen, and work stopped. Because the carving never began, it is the plainest temple in Angkor, made of huge, smoothly cut greenish sandstone blocks, which makes the scale and geometry stand out. The steep stairs up its five tiers lead to a central tower more than 20 m above the ground, with views across the forest. It is usually quiet even when Ta Prohm next door is crowded.
tips: The east stairs are the easiest climb (there is a wooden staircase on part of it); go slowly on the way down.
Take the forest dirt road from Angkor Wat's east gate rather than the main road: it is shaded and almost empty.
stops.from_previous: On foot from Angkor Wat's east gate: about 4.8 km by the forest track and road, 60 min

video.title: Ta Keo Temple - Angkor's Grandest Unfinished Masterpiece

stops.name: Ta Prohm
stops.description: Ta Prohm was founded in 1186 by King Jayavarman VII as a Buddhist monastery dedicated to his mother; an inscription says it once had over 12,000 residents. When restoration began, the French chose to leave much of it as it was found, so silk-cotton and strangler fig trees still grow out of its towers and walls, their roots pouring over the stone. Today you follow wooden walkways through collapsed courtyards and dark corridors; some areas are propped up by the Archaeological Survey of India, which is restoring it. It is famous from the film Tomb Raider and is one of the most atmospheric places at Angkor.
tips: Enter by the quiet north gate (a few minutes from Ta Keo) and leave by the east gate, which puts you 600 m from Banteay Kdei.
Midday is busy; the famous 'Tomb Raider' tree (inner east courtyard) has a queue for photos. Look for the less-photographed roots in the outer galleries instead.
Stick to the marked paths: several sections are fenced off because of falling stones.
stops.from_previous: On foot from Ta Keo: about 1.2 km to Ta Prohm's north gate, 15 min

video.title: Amazing abandoned temple with trees in the jungle of Cambodia | Ta Prohm Temple Walking Tour | 4K

stops.name: Banteay Kdei and Srah Srang (with lunch)
stops.description: Banteay Kdei ('Citadel of the Monks' Cells') is another late-12th-century Buddhist monastery by Jayavarman VII, built in the same Bayon style as Ta Prohm but more open and much quieter. You walk in a straight line through four enclosures, past face-towers on the gates, dancing apsara carvings and half-collapsed galleries with trees growing through them. Its east gate opens onto Srah Srang, the 'Royal Bath', a 700 m-long reservoir dug in the 10th century with a sandstone landing stage guarded by lions and nagas. Srah Srang is a calm place to rest by the water, and the food stalls opposite are the natural lunch stop.
tips: Walk through Banteay Kdei from west to east and come out directly at Srah Srang.
Lunch at the restaurants across the road from Srah Srang (rice and noodle dishes US$4–6); confirm prices before ordering.
Srah Srang is also a peaceful sunrise spot (open from 05:00) — an option for the last morning on Thu 14.
stops.from_previous: On foot from Ta Prohm's east gate: 600 m, 8 min

video.title: Banteay Kdei Temple Tour 4K - Siem Reap Cambodia 2023

stops.name: East Mebon
stops.description: East Mebon was dedicated in 953 AD by King Rajendravarman to Shiva and to his parents. It stood on an artificial island in the middle of the East Baray, a 7 km by 1.8 km reservoir that is now dry rice fields, and boats would have landed at its four sides. Life-size stone elephants stand on the corners of its terraces, and five brick towers with fine lintel carvings crown the top. It is spacious, warm-coloured and usually close to empty.
tips: Look for the elephants on the corners of the first and second terraces; the one at the south-west corner is the best preserved.
Walking from Srah Srang is possible (1.8 km to Pre Rup, then 1.5 km to East Mebon) but the road is open and hot: take the tuk-tuk.
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from Srah Srang: 3.2 km, 10 min (pickup arranged for the afternoon, about US$10–15 including the ride back to town)
stops.image_credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File%3AEast_Mebon_%289713398037%29.jpg

video.title: 4K | East Mebon Temple Walking tour | Mountain temple in the center of the East baray

stops.name: Banteay Samre
stops.description: Banteay Samre is a mid-12th-century Hindu temple from the same period as Angkor Wat, on the far side of the old East Baray. It was heavily restored by French archaeologists in the 1940s, so it is one of the most complete small temples in the park: raised walkways, sunken courtyards, a central tower and crisp carved lintels with scenes from the Ramayana. Its name refers to the Samré, a local people, and a legend about a cucumber-farming king. Few tour groups come this far, so it is usually peaceful in the late afternoon.
tips: Only worth it if you still have energy: it adds about 40 minutes of tuk-tuk riding.
The inner courtyard is surrounded by a raised gallery; walk the whole circuit for the best lintels.
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from East Mebon: about 5 km, 12 min

video.title: The Timeless Elegance of the Banteay Samre Temple, Siem Reap, Cambodia 2023

stops.name: Pre Rup at sunset
stops.description: Pre Rup was built in 961 AD by King Rajendravarman as his state temple, a pyramid of laterite and red brick with five towers on top. The name means 'turning the body', from a later belief that cremations took place here. At sunset the brick glows deep orange and you look west over rice fields and palm trees towards the forest, without the crowds of Phnom Bakheng. It is one of the best places for a quiet end to a long temple day.
tips: Climb to the top level by 17:20 to get a good spot on the west side; the sun sets at about 17:55.
Stairs are steep and narrow; bring a phone light for the way down after sunset.
Ask your tuk-tuk to wait at the east entrance car park, then ride 14 km (25 min) back to town.
stops.from_previous: Tuk-tuk from Banteay Samre: about 6 km, 15 min (or 1.3 km from East Mebon, 3 min)

video.title: AMAZING SUNSET VIEWS at Angkor Wat | Pre Rup Temple

backup_ideas.name: Chao Phraya Sky Park
backup_ideas.blurb: A landscaped pedestrian park built on the unfinished pillars of an abandoned 1980s skytrain bridge, crossing the river high above the water. From the middle you get open views of the river, Memorial Bridge and the Thonburi and Old Town skylines.

backup_ideas.name: Wat Chedi Luang & Wat Phan Tao after dark (plus monk chat)
backup_ideas.blurb: The ruined 15th-century chedi of Wat Chedi Luang (once the tallest structure in Lanna, cracked by a 1545 earthquake) is floodlit at night and nearly empty after the tour groups leave. Next door, the all-teak hall of Wat Phan Tao glows with lanterns. Come in the afternoon first for the free monk chat tables on the grounds, then stay for dusk.

backup_ideas.name: New Year's Eve fireworks (31 Dec 2026)
backup_ideas.blurb: KL rings in the New Year with fireworks over the Petronas Towers, a countdown in KLCC Park, a light show and parties around Bukit Bintang and KL Tower. Last year's (2025/26) events included Rhythm of KLCC, a 10-minute fireworks show at Pavilion and a KL Tower countdown.

backup_ideas.name: Amazing Thailand Countdown 2027 at ICONSIAM
backup_ideas.note: great, but i get IN on the 1st, so not sure if thats too late for part of the festival
backup_ideas.blurb: Bangkok's biggest New Year celebration runs as a five-day festival at ICONSIAM's River Park with concerts and drone shows, ending with a 1,400 m fireworks display along the Chao Phraya at midnight on 31 December. Watch from the river park, a rooftop, a riverside hotel or a dinner cruise.

backup_ideas.name: Phetchaburi: Khao Wang palace & Khao Luang cave
backup_ideas.blurb: Ride a cable car up Khao Wang to Phra Nakhon Khiri, King Rama IV's hilltop palace and temples with views over the town and paddies. Then visit Tham Khao Luang, a cave temple where sunbeams fall through the roof onto rows of Buddha images, and Wat Yai Suwannaram's Ayutthaya-era murals.

backup_ideas.name: National Museum of Royal Barges
backup_ideas.blurb: A boat shed on the Bangkok Noi canal holding the gilded royal barges used in the rare Royal Barge Procession, including the 46 m Suphannahong with its swan-head prow. It's small but striking, and reaching it through a stilt-house lane by the canal is half the fun.

backup_ideas.name: Wat Ratchabophit
backup_ideas.blurb: A royal temple from 1869 where everything is covered in multicolored Chinese ceramic tiles, around a circular cloister and a gilded chedi. The ordination hall's doors are inlaid with mother-of-pearl, and the interior surprises with a Gothic, European-style chapel. Next door is a little-visited royal cemetery with Khmer, Gothic and Thai-style memorials.

backup_ideas.name: Chiang Rai: White Temple, Blue Temple & Baan Dam
backup_ideas.note: exciting, but far. If i end up having on the higher end for number of days, I'll add. In general, worth adding to our final writeup in case I have extra time.
backup_ideas.blurb: Three striking modern art temples: the all-white Wat Rong Khun with its mirror mosaics, the sapphire-and-gold Wat Rong Suea Ten, and Baan Dam (Black House), an eerie complex of dark teak buildings by artist Thawan Duchanee. Add the Saturday/Sunday walking streets or Singha Park tea fields if you stay over.

backup_ideas.name: Wat Ban Den (Wat Den Sali Si Mueang Kaen)
backup_ideas.blurb: A sprawling hillside temple complex of dazzling Lanna-style halls, gilded roofs and 12 zodiac chedis, built over decades by a revered local abbot. Locals visit their birth-year chedi; you wander between ornate wooden and mirrored buildings with mountain views behind.

backup_ideas.name: KL Forest Eco Park canopy walk (Bukit Nanas)
backup_ideas.blurb: Malaysia's oldest protected forest (gazetted 1906), a patch of real rainforest in the middle of the city. A canopy walkway of suspended bridges runs through the treetops with glimpses of KL Tower and the skyscrapers, and short trails lead past giant trees and macaque troops.

backup_ideas.name: Baphuon, Preah Palilay & Tep Pranam
backup_ideas.blurb: Baphuon is an 11th-century temple-mountain with a 200 m raised walkway; it was taken apart by French archaeologists and rebuilt like a giant jigsaw, and its west side forms a huge reclining Buddha. Behind it in the forest sit Preah Palilay, a lonely tree-shaded sanctuary, and Tep Pranam, a large seated Buddha still used by nuns and worshippers.

backup_ideas.name: Khao Sok: Cheow Lan Lake floating bungalows
backup_ideas.blurb: An emerald reservoir inside one of the world's oldest rainforests, ringed by sheer limestone karsts. Sleep in a bamboo raft house on the water, kayak at dawn while gibbons call, swim off your porch, and hike to jungle caves such as Nam Talu.

backup_ideas.name: Sukhothai & Si Satchanalai
backup_ideas.blurb: Thailand's first capital (13th–15th century), a UNESCO park of lotus ponds, lotus-bud chedis and serene walking Buddhas that you explore by bicycle. Its twin city Si Satchanalai, an hour north, is quieter still: overgrown temples like Wat Chang Lom ringed with elephant statues, where you may be the only visitor.

backup_ideas.name: Kanchanaburi & the Death Railway
backup_ideas.note: Interesting (want to know more), but have to weigh against other day trips
backup_ideas.blurb: See the Bridge over the River Kwai, the moving Thailand–Burma Railway Centre and the Allied war cemetery, then ride the WWII 'Death Railway' train along the cliff-hugging Wang Pho (Tham Krasae) viaduct above the river. With an early start a driver can add Hellfire Pass or Erawan Falls.

backup_ideas.name: Khlong Saen Saep canal boat ride
backup_ideas.blurb: The commuter canal express that roars along a narrow canal between Old Town and the modern centre; you pull a tarp up against splashes while passing stilt houses, mosques and high-rises. Ride from Phan Fa Lilat pier near the Golden Mount to Pratunam, then change for Asok.

backup_ideas.name: Koh Kret island
backup_ideas.blurb: A car-free island in the Chao Phraya, home to a Mon community known for terracotta pottery. Walk or cycle the 6 km loop past potteries, the leaning white chedi of Wat Poramai Yikawat and stalls selling Mon desserts and fried flowers.

backup_ideas.name: Lopburi: Khmer ruins and the monkey temple
backup_ideas.note: dont think i would do this in addition to ayutthaya but curious to learn more especially about the monkeys
backup_ideas.blurb: An ancient Khmer and Ayutthaya-era town centred on Phra Prang Sam Yot, three linked 13th-century laterite towers ruled by hundreds of macaques. Also see the large Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat ruins and King Narai's 17th-century palace, now a museum.

backup_ideas.name: Nakhon Pathom: Phra Pathom Chedi & Sanam Chandra Palace
backup_ideas.blurb: Phra Pathom Chedi, at 120 m one of the tallest stupas in the world, marks where Buddhism may first have arrived in Thailand; walk its cloisters and terraces. Nearby, the peaceful Sanam Chandra Palace of King Rama VI mixes Thai and English-Tudor buildings in a huge park.

backup_ideas.name: Talat Noi & Song Wat Road
backup_ideas.blurb: A maze of old Hokkien lanes full of car-parts workshops, street art, shrines and the 200-year-old So Heng Tai courtyard mansion, plus the Holy Rosary Church and riverside cafés. Continue up Song Wat Road, a row of restored shophouses with spice traders, coffee bars and galleries.

backup_ideas.name: Mon Cham (Mon Jam) & Mae Sa valley
backup_ideas.blurb: A Hmong highland project on a ridge at ~1,400 m with flower and vegetable terraces, tent campsites and wide views over the Mae Sa valley. The drive up the winding Mae Sa road passes waterfalls and strawberry farms; sunrise brings a sea of mist on cold mornings.

backup_ideas.name: Queen Sirikit Botanic Garden & canopy walkway
backup_ideas.blurb: Thailand's leading botanic garden spread across forested hills, with a ~400 m canopy walkway about 20 m above the trees, glasshouses of orchids and lotus, and quiet trails. Views stretch over the Mae Sa valley and Doi Suthep range.

backup_ideas.name: Wua Lai Saturday walking street
backup_ideas.blurb: The Saturday night market on the old silversmith street is smaller and more local than the famous Sunday market. Stalls sell food, crafts and silverwork, and Wat Sri Suphan glows silver at the end of the street.

backup_ideas.name: Brickfields (Little India) temple walk
backup_ideas.blurb: KL's most vibrant Indian quarter: banana-leaf rice restaurants, flower-garland stalls and Tamil music along Jalan Tun Sambanthan. Within a few blocks are the Sri Kandaswamy Kovil (a Sri Lankan Tamil temple), the Buddhist Maha Vihara (founded 1894) and old churches, showing KL's many faiths side by side.

backup_ideas.name: TRX City Park (rooftop park at The Exchange TRX)
backup_ideas.blurb: A 10-acre landscaped park on the roof of The Exchange TRX mall, opened in late 2023, with lawns, water features and walking paths. From here the new skyline towers over you: Exchange 106 right above and Merdeka 118 in the distance.

backup_ideas.name: Angkor Thom wall walk & quiet gates
backup_ideas.blurb: The 8 m-high earth wall around Angkor Thom has a shaded path on top that you can walk or cycle. Along it are the small Prasat Chrung corner shrines, and the far-less-visited North Gate, Victory Gate and Gate of the Dead, each topped with giant stone faces.

backup_ideas.name: Terrace of the Elephants & Leper King (hidden inner wall)
backup_ideas.blurb: The long royal viewing terrace with its parade of carved elephants, and the Terrace of the Leper King beside it. The real secret is the narrow trench between the outer wall and an older inner wall, where you walk past rows of deeply cut, almost untouched carvings of nagas, kings, apsaras and sea creatures.

backup_ideas.name: Phnom Krom sunset
backup_ideas.blurb: A 140 m hill crowned by three late-9th-century sandstone towers and a working pagoda. From the top you look over the Tonle Sap lake, flooded fields and stilt villages, and the sun sets over the water.

backup_ideas.name: Overnight sleeper train Bangkok → Chiang Mai
backup_ideas.blurb: Thailand's classic rail journey on the Chinese-built sleeper cars (in service since 2016): staff make up your bunk after dinner, and you wake to the train climbing through teak forests and the Khun Tan tunnel into the northern hills. Upgrade option: the restored 1960s 'Blue Jasmine' train (launched Nov 2025) runs a 9-day luxury Bangkok–Chiang Mai journey with stops at Ayutthaya, Uthai Thani and Sukhothai.

backup_ideas.name: Bang Krachao by bike ('Bangkok's green lung')
backup_ideas.blurb: A jungle-covered loop of the Chao Phraya where 2 m-wide raised concrete paths wind through mangroves, banana groves and stilt villages. Rent a bike at the pier, ride to Sri Nakhon Khuean Khan Park with its lake and birdwatching tower, and stop at canal-side cafés; on weekends visit Bang Nam Phueng floating market.

backup_ideas.name: Bang Pa-In Royal Palace
backup_ideas.blurb: A royal summer palace on a river island with an elegant Thai pavilion floating in a pond, a Chinese-style throne hall and European mansions in manicured gardens. Nearby, Wat Niwet Thammaprawat is a Buddhist temple built to look like a Gothic church, reached by a cable-pulled cart-ferry.

backup_ideas.name: Bangkokian Museum
backup_ideas.blurb: A family's 1930s wooden house and garden kept exactly as it was, showing how a middle-class Bangkok household lived before the high-rises. Rooms of furniture, records, kitchenware and photos, plus a doctor's surgery building, all in a shady garden off Charoen Krung.

backup_ideas.name: Museum Siam
backup_ideas.blurb: A modern, interactive museum in a grand colonial-era ministry building that asks 'what does it mean to be Thai?' through playful rooms on history, food, beliefs and identity. In 2026–27 it is also a Bangkok Art Biennale venue with contemporary installations.

backup_ideas.name: Nang Loeng Market
backup_ideas.blurb: Thailand's first land market (1900), a covered wooden market in an old community with stalls of traditional Thai desserts, curries over rice and noodles. Look for the century-old khanom thuai stall and the old cinema façade; nearby lanes are home to families of classical dancers and musicians.

backup_ideas.name: Phra Sumen Fort, Santi Chai Prakan Park & Phra Athit Road
backup_ideas.blurb: A whitewashed 1783 octagonal fort, one of two survivors of the old city walls, stands in a small riverside park with views of the Rama VIII cable-stayed bridge. Locals jog and do aerobics at dusk, and Phra Athit Road behind it has old shophouses, bars with live music and small restaurants.

backup_ideas.name: Wat Suthat & the Giant Swing
backup_ideas.blurb: One of Bangkok's six first-class royal temples, with a vast ordination hall, huge wall murals and the 8 m bronze Phra Si Sakyamuni Buddha brought from Sukhothai. Out front stands the red teak Giant Swing, once used in a Brahmin swinging ceremony, and the surrounding streets sell bronze Buddha images and monk supplies.

backup_ideas.name: Ban Tawai woodcarving village
backup_ideas.blurb: A long-established crafts village of open workshops where carvers make Lanna-style wood carvings, furniture and lacquerware. Walk the lanes and watch the artisans at work; it pairs well with Wat Inthrawat nearby.

backup_ideas.name: Bo Sang umbrella village & Umbrella Festival
backup_ideas.blurb: Bo Sang is the home of hand-painted paper and cotton umbrellas; workshops show every step from bamboo frame to painting. During the festival the village street is hung with hundreds of umbrellas, with parades, crafts and a 'Miss Bo Sang' on bicycles holding umbrellas. Nearby San Kamphaeng has silk and celadon workshops and the MAIIAM contemporary art museum.

backup_ideas.name: Doi Mae Salong (Santikhiri)
backup_ideas.blurb: A mountaintop village founded by Chinese Kuomintang soldiers who fled Yunnan in 1949, now surrounded by oolong tea terraces. Drink tea at plantations like 101 Tea, eat Yunnanese noodles, walk the morning market with Akha and Lisu traders, and climb to the Princess Mother's chedi for the view.

backup_ideas.name: Huai Nam Dang: Doi Kiew Lom sea of mist & Pong Duet hot springs
backup_ideas.blurb: Doi Kiew Lom viewpoint at the park headquarters looks over rolling ridges toward Doi Luang Chiang Dao, and in the cool season the valleys fill with a sea of mist at dawn. On the way back, Pong Duet has boiling geysers and natural hot pools in the forest for a soak.

backup_ideas.name: Huay Tung Tao Lake
backup_ideas.blurb: A reservoir at the foot of Doi Suthep lined with bamboo huts on stilts where you lounge over the water and order grilled fish, som tam and cold drinks. Giant straw sculptures sit around the lake, and a paved loop is good for a bike ride or short walk.

backup_ideas.name: Lampang: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang & old town
backup_ideas.blurb: Wat Phra That Lampang Luang is a walled 13th–15th-century hilltop temple, perhaps the finest surviving Lanna wooden temple, famous for a pinhole image of the chedi projected upside down in a dark hall. Lampang town has teak mansions like Baan Sao Nak, horse-drawn carriages and a Sunday walking street along the river.

backup_ideas.name: Phu Chi Fa sunrise
backup_ideas.blurb: A knife-edge cliff at ~1,600 m jutting out toward Laos, where a sea of clouds fills the Mekong valley at dawn. A 20–30 minute walk from the village takes you to the point in the dark; you watch the sun rise over the clouds.

backup_ideas.name: Warorot Market & Ton Lam Yai flower market
backup_ideas.blurb: Chiang Mai's main local market (Kad Luang): three floors of northern sausages, chili pastes, dried fruit, hill-tribe textiles and household goods. Across the street, Ton Lam Yai flower market is busiest at night with marigold garlands for the temples.

backup_ideas.name: Wat Inthrawat (Wat Ton Kwen)
backup_ideas.blurb: A small, carefully preserved 1850s Lanna temple in a village setting: a teak wihan with sweeping layered roofs and a rare open-sided pavilion (mondop) that once sheltered a Buddha relic during processions. It is regarded as one of the best examples of original Lanna wooden architecture left.

backup_ideas.name: Wiang Kum Kam ancient city
backup_ideas.blurb: The first capital of King Mengrai (late 1200s), abandoned after floods and buried under river silt until the 1980s. More than 20 excavated temple ruins sit among village lanes and rice fields; you explore by bicycle, horse cart or small tram, stopping at Wat Chedi Liam (a working temple with a stepped Mon-style chedi) and Wat Kan Thom.

backup_ideas.name: Old Kuala Lumpur Railway Station
backup_ideas.blurb: A 1910 Indo-Saracenic railway station of white domes, minarets and arches, facing the equally ornate KTM headquarters across the road. The front was restored in 2026 and the government has just announced a fuller restoration for tourism; it is still a working Komuter stop, so you can wander the old platforms.

backup_ideas.name: Pulau Ketam (Crab Island) fishing village
backup_ideas.blurb: A Chinese fishing village built on stilts over mangrove mudflats, reached by a 30-45 minute ferry from Port Klang. Walk the plank lanes past colourful houses and temples, rent a bicycle and eat a seafood lunch of crab and chilli prawns.

backup_ideas.name: Puncak Alop (new Ampang hilltop lookout)
backup_ideas.blurb: A hilltop viewpoint above the old Ampang Lookout that reopened in March 2026 after a full redevelopment. The main platform, Puncak Hauz, looks across the whole skyline: Petronas Towers, Merdeka 118, Exchange 106 and KL Tower, with a cafe and restaurant on site.

backup_ideas.name: Phnom Kulen
backup_ideas.blurb: The mountain where Jayavarman II declared the Khmer Empire in 802 AD. Visit carved riverbed lingas, the 16th-century reclining Buddha on top of a boulder at Preah Ang Thom, and swim at the two-level waterfall; with a motorbike guide you can reach forest-covered temples like Prasat Rong Chen.

backup_ideas.name: Quad or dirt-bike ride to villages at sunset
backup_ideas.blurb: Guided rides on red dirt tracks through rice paddies, stilt-house villages and small pagodas, ending with sunset over the fields. Options run from 1.5-hour quad loops to half-day dirt-bike rides further out.

backup_ideas.name: Ta Som
backup_ideas.blurb: A small late-12th-century temple of Jayavarman VII with Bayon-style face towers on its gates. The famous sight is the eastern gate, almost swallowed by a huge strangler fig. Inside are quiet, crumbling galleries with well-kept devata carvings.

backup_ideas.name: Kampot & Kep (with the Phnom Penh–Kampot train)
backup_ideas.blurb: Kampot is a sleepy riverside town of faded French shophouses, sunset river cruises and Kampot pepper farms. Above it, Bokor Mountain holds an abandoned 1920s French hill station with a ghostly church and palace hotel; nearby Kep is a seaside village known for crab fresh from the market and boats to Rabbit Island.

backup_ideas.name: Kuching & Bako (Malaysian Borneo)
backup_ideas.blurb: A relaxed riverside city with a white-rajah history, Chinese temples and colonial forts. From here you can see semi-wild orangutans at Semenggoh, hike the coastal jungle of Bako National Park to spot proboscis monkeys, and visit a Bidayuh longhouse at Annah Rais.

backup_ideas.name: Nan (northern Thailand)
backup_ideas.blurb: A sleepy, old Lanna-era city in a green valley, famous for the 19th-century murals of Wat Phumin (including the 'whispering' couple) and the gold chedi of Wat Phra That Chae Haeng. Rent a scooter or hire a driver for the Sapan village rice terraces, the ancient Bo Kluea mountain salt wells and the sea-of-fog viewpoint at Doi Samer Dao.

backup_ideas.name: Penang: George Town
backup_ideas.blurb: A UNESCO-listed trading port of Chinese clan houses, Peranakan mansions, mosques, Hindu temples and colonial streets, all walkable. Explore the Khoo Kongsi clan temple and the clan jetties on stilts, eat at the hawker stalls (Penang is Malaysia's food capital), ride the funicular up Penang Hill and visit the huge Kek Lok Si temple.
